text.en: The Mashgiach holds that a wish is only the reason a person turns to Hashem; once he turns, the purpose of the tefillah is the closeness itself, so it succeeds even if the wish is not granted.
Asking Hashem for something insignificant, like a maid not quitting, is not a lowering of one's avodah but the peak of emunah, a declaration that Hashem controls every detail.

Unlike the angels and the creatures of Perek Shirah, who sing at fixed times, a Jew needs no appointment: he may sing to Hashem whenever he calls to Him, which is why the words 'tzafra' and 'ramsha' are named for the singing of the birds and creeping things.
The Mashgiach's Rebbe read the Ba'al Shem Tov's 'teivah' as the ark of Noach: the world is a flood of turmoil, and the word of davening is the refuge in which a person is saved.
A sudden good davening may be the reward of a nisayon a person withstood a day or a week before; it is a gift, a free taste, but lasting good davening must be earned.

The Mashgiach reads the Gemara's twelve thousand pairs of talmidim as chavrusas in which the stronger partner looked down on the weaker; the cure is knowing that every Jew carries a hidden secret no other Jew can accomplish.
Yerushalayim is written hundreds of times without its second yud because it cannot be complete while Rome stands; only when Moshiach comes will it be written full, with the yud.
The sun is not Esav's by right: it was created for Yisrael and is only harnessed for now to Esav's wagon of nature, while Esav himself only mimics Yaakov like a monkey and is in truth a mirage.
Chametz is one of Esav's aliases, so burning chametz on Erev Pesach is destroying Amalek, whose soul is the yetzer hara.
In the side of impurity the female force is stronger than the male, the reverse of holiness, which is why the nations let the lady go first while Jews put right over left.
The 28-year cycle of the sun is its yovel, just as the fiftieth year is the yovel of a Jew: nature has 28 levels, the 28 times of Koheles and the 28 letters of the first passuk of the Torah.
No brachah is made over the sun on its daily or yearly rounds because it is then in Esav's service; only once in 28 years, at its point of origin, does it belong to Yaakov and can be blessed.
When time returns to its origin, the first 'time to be born' of Koheles, Moshiach is born; this is why his coming is called a birth and the suffering before it 'the birth pangs of Moshiach'.
Because Klal Yisrael accepted Pesukei d'Zimra and Maariv on itself, the Mashgiach suggests they may in some way be a bigger obligation than the other tefillos, carrying the force of a vow.

The more kedushah a thing holds, the thicker the tumah around it: bread needs more mitzvos than other food, the Bris is covered by the orlah, Eretz Yisrael was held by the Canaanites, and a tzaddik has a bigger yetzer.
The later chumros in kashrus and the longer davening of later generations stem from one cause: a lower generation needs more refined food and more tefillah to purify itself.
'HaMelech' in the Megillah equals Haman in gematria and also 'Kes Kah', the incomplete throne: while Haman reigns, Hashem's kingship shows only as Yud-Kei without Vav-Kei.
By At-Bash, the Mem and Tzadi of 'mitzvah' stand for Yud and Hei, so the word itself is Yud-Kei hidden and Vav-Kei revealed, making every mitzvah a yichud of the hidden and the revealed.
On Purim we wear masks because Hashem acts in this world in a masquerade; the point of Purim is to rip off that mask and recognize Him.
The Mashgiach explains that the word tefillah itself means attachment, from the word tafel, so that tefillah is by definition dveikus to Hashem.

According to the Mashgiach, arguing whether Torah or tefillah is greater is like arguing whether the brain or the heart is more important: other mitzvos are like a finger one can live without, but these two are the vital organs.
The Mashgiach says that one who davens with real dveikus davens slowly not by design but because he cannot bring himself to leave a word that means so much to him.

The Mashgiach reads the sudden explosion of inventions in the last two hundred years, after thousands of years without progress, as the Satan's final struggle before Moshiach, like a candle flaring up just before it goes out.
The Mashgiach sees the physical pollution of air, water and food as a reflection of the spiritual contamination of the atmosphere caused by more aveiros.
From the radio, which shows that the atmosphere holds whatever is put into it, the Mashgiach learns that every word of Torah sanctifies the atmosphere and every bad word contaminates it.
The Mashgiach compares this generation to the best soldiers, whom an army sends to the most dangerous front: being born now is a mark of trust and a shlichus no earlier generation had.
Since kavanah in Avos is a return to the root of the soul in the Avos, the Mashgiach ties it to learning Sefer Bereishis: one who does not know the Avos cannot truly have kavanah in Avos.
Yetzias Mitzrayim contains the redemptions of all generations and of every individual, so remembering it is a means by which a Jew can merit his own yeshuah.

The spiritual exile of Mitzrayim was a closed heart that could not daven, the same blockage a person feels in davening today; the Exodus, Pesach as 'the mouth that speaks', opened the gates of tefillah.
Emes V'yatziv is the staircase to Shemoneh Esrei: its fifteen words beginning with vav are the fifteen steps of the Beis HaMikdash and the fifteen Shir HaMaalos.
The four times 'emes' after the mention of the Exodus correspond to the four exiles, since the Exodus already carries the power to redeem from all four.
Of the three kinds of tefillah, of Moshe, of David and of the poor man, the poor man's broken-hearted tefillah 'wraps around' all the others and accomplishes the most.

Yaakov Avinu deliberately used his weakest bracha for his own troubles and reserved the stronger three for the troubles before Moshiach, so the present danger is the very time those brachos were kept for.
The seventy words of Lamenatzeach correspond to the seventy sighs of a woman in labor, and since the generation is in the birth pangs of Moshiach, it has reached the last word, kareinu.
Lamenatzeach means both 'to the conductor' of the singers and 'to the One who grants victory': Dovid sings to Hashem as the One who assures victory, and so he thanks Him even before the yeshua.
Only when a person has run out of his own eitzos, as in ad anah ashis eitzos, does Hashem's salvation have to appear.
Hashem is called Elokei Yaakov in a time of trouble because Yaakov's whole life was one chain of troubles borne with bitachon, and he stands for the Jewish people's long journey through galus.
The tzaddikim's pain in their troubles is not for themselves but that Hashem's Name is not complete, so their request is that His Name become whole.
The word va'nisoded comes from 'od', 'still': nations that fall stay fallen, but the Jewish people's fall is only temporary because they are eternal.

Although one normally listens to the chazzan's repetition and answers, at Modim each person says Modim d'Rabbanan himself, because thanking Hashem brings such closeness that one does not let another do it for him.
The Mashgiach reads the close of Modim d'Rabbanan as thanks for the very ability and desire to thank, which Hashem places in a person's heart.
The rescue that obligates thanks is a reminder: being delivered from one trouble should make a person thank Hashem for all the troubles he was never put into.
Birkas HaGomel needs two Rabbanan: one chacham to explain Hashem's kindness, and a second to show that after the first seemed to finish, there was still more to say.
The korban todah's short eating time forces its owner to invite more people, so the thanksgiving becomes a greater kiddush shem shamayim.

Knowing that one owes thanks makes a person subordinate to his benefactor; therefore the more he appreciates Hashem's goodness, the more he becomes a tzaddik who cannot bring himself to displease Him.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem gave up the fitting punishment at the Nile so that the miracle would happen where Jews could return and make a bracha.

The Mashgiach reads Adam HaRishon's first conversation with Hashem, blaming the wife Hashem gave him, as ingratitude, and sees Bikurim, the first of the gifts, as its direct opposite: a declaration that one is not ungrateful.
The hundred daily brachos parallel Mizmor Lesodah being the hundredth chapter of Tehillim: a hundred thanks each day.
The word Ish, used for a bar mitzvah, stands for ahavah, yirah and simcha, the three things with which a grown Jew serves Hashem.
A korban brought for a sin lacked joy, so the song of the Levi'im supplied the simcha; Mizmor Lesodah teaches a person not to rely on others but to bring joy to his own service.
The devar halacha before davening is meant to be a clear halacha, because nothing gives simcha like understanding a piece of Gemara clearly, and that joy prepares a person for tefillah.
The letters of the word bracha each show a doubling: beis is one become two, chaf is ten become twenty, and reish is a hundred become two hundred.

Yavan is the opposite of Yosef: Yosef is addition in kedushah, Yavan is addition in tumah that invades what is not its own, and the letters yud, vav, nun, each an extension of the one before, show this.
On Chanukah the Jews in turn enter the domain of tumah: the lights are lit in the darkness of night, at the left side of the door, which represents the sitra achra and the public domain.
Placing 'evening, morning and afternoon' after 'Your miracles that are with us every day' carries a second intention: that there are miracles three times every day.
The whole month of Kislev is Chanukah: the twenty-four days before it belong to the twenty-fifth, which the Mashgiach links to Shema Yisrael and mesiras nefesh.
Reading the offerings of the twelve Nesi'im on Chanukah is a zechus against the twelve princes of Yishmael.
The Mashgiach reads the Kaddeishim of Shacharis as markers between the worlds: a Kaddish is said each time one passes from one world to another, going up and coming down.

The second half of davening, after Shemoneh Esrei, is the bringing down of the shefa that was asked for; like paying in a store and leaving the goods on the counter, one who neglects it brings nothing home.
Because the words of davening were composed with ruach hakodesh, they effect great tikkunim even when the one davening does not know the kavanos, provided he davens properly.
Waking each morning is like birth: as the yetzer hara reaches a child years before the yetzer tov, it reaches a person first each morning, which is why Modeh Ani must come at once.
Modeh Ani was composed without a Name of Hashem precisely so that it could be said before washing, letting the very first word and thought of the day be thanks to Hashem.

Just as no day repeats another's task, no Jew was created to do what another does; Hashem guides the parents to choose a name that fits the soul's shlichus, and every Jew also has a name from the sitra achra that must be nullified.

The Mashgiach explains, recalling the Satmar Rav's drashos, that a leader speaks about the matters his generation particularly needs, while Torah is a general subject; this is why he himself speaks about tefillah.
The davening in the beis medrash was better in its early years because the group was persecuted, which drove them to better tefillos, and because the original members were then the majority.
Tefillah is so great a mitzvah that it is included in kriyas shema itself: within the parsha of accepting the mitzvos, 'to serve Him with all your heart' stands as the example of a mitzvah.
Since pigul shows that a mere thought can disqualify a korban, and tefillah stands in place of the korbanos, the Mashgiach derives that thought is the decisive part of tefillah.
Saying the words without kavanah fulfills only the rabbinic enactment of three tefillos, not the Torah mitzvah of serving Hashem with the heart.
Kavanah itself is a gift from Hashem, as the passuk says that He prepares their heart and then listens, so one must daven to be able to daven with kavanah.

Citing the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thoughts are, the Mashgiach explains that one who faces Yerushalayim in prayer is truly there, before the Kodesh HaKodashim, standing before the King.

The Mashgiach's rebbe joins the Ba'al Shem Tov's drush to the plain meaning: the flood is the world itself, whose 'arks' of pleasure and honor swallow people, and the true ark of rescue is the word of prayer.

The Mashgiach reads the Gemara's 'things that stand at the height of the world, which people treat lightly' as the very sign of tefillah's greatness: that good davening is mocked while good learning is praised shows how high prayer reaches.
Loud davening is both a proclamation before Hashem that we are His creations, as the Ramban writes, and a weapon: shouting over the yetzer hara, who argues for a quick and easy davening.
Pushing a slow chazzan from the amud is not merely impatience: since lengthening prayer lengthens life, the hurried worshipper drives away the long life of those who want to daven at length.

The order of a person's life mirrors the order of history: just as a person begins with Torah and later turns to avodah, the early generations' main avodah was Torah, while in the time before Moshiach it is tefillah.

The Mashgiach reads the Ba'al HaTanya's demand that all say each word together in light of the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that each word is a heichal: saying the same word at once puts the whole tzibbur in one heichal.
Lashon hakodesh is not only the language of the Torah; according to the Mashgiach one can speak 'in lashon hakodesh' even in Yiddish, as tzaddikim speak words that carry hidden depths.
A foreign thought in the middle of davening, such as what shoes to buy for Yom Tov, pushes a person out of the heichal of the word he is saying.
Loud communal davening works like the angels, who receive from one another: even a person who walks in without enthusiasm gets an 'injection' from the tzibbur and begins to daven well.
The Mashgiach contrasts the crowd that shouts over a home run with those who resent shouting in davening, the privilege of standing before Ribono shel Olam.
A promise from Hashem does not remove the need for tefillah: Eliyahu was told it would rain and still had to daven for it.
The Mashgiach contrasts the other side's wonder at the rocket that did not explode with our own lack of surprise, since we know Hashem is making miracles for us.
Precisely because miracles are visible now, the Mashgiach weighs whether the custom of freely omitting Tachanun for distant yahrtzeits fits such a time.
A creature's true place is shown by where it runs when chased; so too a Jew's true belonging is revealed when, in danger, he runs to the Ribono shel Olam.
Honoring a tzaddik's yahrtzeit does not override the need to say Tachanun when the Jewish people need a yeshuah.
Seeing miracles is no reason to stop asking for mercy.
Tefillah is not in competition with Torah: a little closeness to Hashem in davening changes the way one learns the entire day.
The Mashgiach reads the Haggadah's use of the pesukim of the bikkurim declaration as a lesson that redemption comes through crying out, which is the call of the present time.
Being chosen for Eretz Yisrael when many are not is itself a cause of greater obligation, not only of joy.
Habits brought from abroad, like spitting on the ground, take on a new seriousness in Eretz Yisrael, whose earth one should rather kiss.
Noach planted his vineyard to make kiddush and drink Eliyahu's cup of the rectified world; instead he became drunk, and 'vayishkar' equals 'kos shel Eliyahu Hanavi' in gematria.
Noach chose the raven on purpose: as one of the sinners in the ark, sending it on a mitzvah mission on Shabbos might repair it and with it the whole sin, but its repair had to wait for Eliyahu.
The lion bit Noach because the ark had been a rectified world where a lion lives on straw; once the sin ruined it, the lion could no longer be satisfied by straw and Noach lost his heavenly help.
Moshe Rabbeinu was a gilgul of Noach, and his 'mecheini na' contains 'mei Noach': by giving himself up in prayer for Klal Yisrael he repaired Noach's failure to pray for his generation.
In a dark generation of hester panim, a Jew who still turns to Hashem in prayer makes his emunah shine more than that of earlier, greater generations.
Birds sing in the morning ('tzafra') and insects at night ('ramsha'), each at its time, but a Jew sings 'tzafra veramsha', with no limit on when he may turn to Hashem.
Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz explained the Ba'al Shem Tov: today's world is a flood, and just as the teivah saved Noach, the 'teivah', the word of prayer, shelters a Jew from drowning.

The Plishtim's stopping the wells is the cooling of Avraham's living avodah into lifeless habit, a 'mitzvas anashim melumadah'; Yitzchak's re-digging is renewing the very same path with fresh vitality.
Mockery of long davening is not a sign of error: it has always been the lot of those devoted to tefillah, because tefillah stands at the height of the world and people belittle it.
Bilgah's closed window is each person's channel of blessing from his soul's root; when it is blocked, the remedy is a 'bypass': drawing from a friend's open channel until one's own reopens.
Lateness reveals that the service is not dear, and it carries over to the next world: one who comes late here may find his own tikkun arriving too late above.
A shliach tzibbur who starts Hodu softly out of humility errs: a niggun may begin quietly, but the baal tefillah must begin with boldness to lift the congregation.
A fine voice, like every talent, is given for a person's tikkun; refusing to use it for the tzibbur in the name of modesty squanders what Hashem gave for that purpose.
Learning and davening depend on each other: learning purifies the mind so one can daven, and davening purifies the heart so one can learn.
Pesukei dezimra 'cut through' (zemer meaning to cut) the forces that block prayer; it is the war of David, the warrior king, waged with his songs.
The less obligatory a thing is, the dearer it is to Hashem; doing what one need not do shows greater devotion.
In Hallel Hagadol each angel can say only one praise, while a Jew who says them all includes the whole row of angels.
On weekdays the alphabetic blessing has a word per letter, on Shabbos a whole phrase per letter, because Shabbos's added holiness spreads into whole phrases of song.
A person's soul is scattered in many places, and he is led to a place to gather its parts and redeem the souls found there.
When a person is attacked by doubts about a good deed, it is a sign he carries something precious, as robbers ambush only the truck with money.
The first thought on waking to get up and serve Hashem comes from the soul; the second, which talks one out of it, is only a reaction of imagination.
Avodas Hashem is not a tax paid at set times, after which the rest of the day is one's own; the claim 'I may have my own time' is a mistake.
Whether physical activity was for Hashem is revealed retroactively: if after his needs a person turns to Torah, all of it was service; if not, the whole day was empty.
Torah study, though greater, attracts incentives such as honor and recognition, whereas tefillah is purely speaking to Hashem.
Like a sick man who must live on oranges when he cannot eat bread and meat, the weak generation before Moshiach must strengthen itself through tefillah.
Gemara must be learned, not davened, and davening must be davened, not learned.
In early generations Torah alone sufficed, but now the world is old and bent over and its main avodah is tefillah.

Yitzchak's wells were not plain wells but deeds through which he worked toward the 'living waters', which is Hashem Himself; learning the Torah's account of the wells teaches that one must toil and dig to reach Him.

Following the Kol Simchah, the Plishtim's stopping of the wells was their declaration that the wells were 'just wells', nothing to learn from; that dismissive mockery is itself what blocks the source.
The earth the Plishtim filled the wells with is the element of afar, the root of laziness, so letzanus leads to laziness, and Yitzchak's re-digging stands for renewing toil in Torah and tefillah.

The Vizhnitzer reads the phrases of Nishmas as levels: the higher a person stands, the less physical motion his tefillah needs, from the yesharim who sing and shout, to the tzaddikim with their lips, the chassidim with their tongue, and the kedoshim whose davening is entirely inward.
Moments of dveikus in tefillah serve as a preparation for Torah: after such a moment a person's learning is different, like one to whom the king has spoken.
A person who would refuse to daven or do mitzvos because he does not yet know the whole Torah shows that his learning is not lishmah, which is why one must interrupt Torah for mitzvos.
Those who daven together are like mountain climbers roped together: when one slips he does not fall, because the others hold him.
The angels can say their praise 'together' only because 'all are beloved', each one loving the other; so too the singers at the sea are called 'yedidim', friends.

A bachur's young years parallel the young years of Klal Yisrael, and just as at the end of the galus the emphasis falls on davening, so a bachur cannot neglect davening even though learning is his main task.

The 24 windows of the mishmaros in the Beis HaMikdash correspond to 24 windows of blessing in heaven, linked to the 24 combinations of the Name Adnus; coming late closes a person's window of chochmah, health, simchah and parnassah.
Everything is measured and counted, measure for measure: a soul that came late to davening and learning in its lifetime comes too late to its own tikkun.
One who comes early to davening and learning helps build the Beis HaMikdash, the reverse of the lateness that contributed to its destruction.
The Mashgiach calls 'I have no time, so I daven quickly' a false calculation: since prolonging tefillah prolongs life, the one short of time is precisely the one who should daven at length.
What allowed early generations to daven briefly was not the size of their minds but their openness: a mind not clouded by sins can daven in a moment.
The end of dybbukim in the Chofetz Chaim's time fits the generation's task: when such things are seen, believing is easy, while the mitzvah of our generation is emunah amid hiddenness.
Though outward dybbukim ceased, the Mashgiach says many people carry inner ones: forces created by sins that block learning, davening and good middos.
Yehuda rather than Yissachar or Levi was sent to prepare Goshen because a place is inaugurated with praise of Hashem, which drives out the opposing forces, and Yehuda's name comes from hodaah.
The Melave Malka is the chanukas habayis of the week: as the seudah of Dovid HaMelech, a descendant of Yehuda, its songs of praise drive out the accusers of the weekday.
Since the coming of Moshiach will reveal lights far greater than at the Exodus, the Mashgiach advises using each immersion in the mikveh to prepare oneself to receive the kedushah of Moshiach.
Eating without a brachah withholds blessing from the world, because the brachah is what draws shefa onto all of creation and all Jews.
A brachah by itself is only half a brachah; its completion is the amen answered to it, so one should say it aloud for others to answer.
Even for mitzvos where the Torah does not require lishmah, declaring one's intent beforehand brings kedushah into both the person and the object, as with tefillin and tzitzis.
Saying 'in the name of all Israel' is an insurance policy for a mitzvah: accusers can attack a private person's deed, but not one bound to all of Klal Yisrael, of whom it says there is no blemish.
Beginning Baruch She'amar with the congregation makes one's whole tefillah count as tefillah b'tzibbur, even if the congregation has left before one reaches Shemoneh Esrei.

The leniency of a doubtful rabbinic law does not show it is lower; the Sages themselves chose to be lenient, like a mother who lets her child try another store, and where they did not want leniency, as with Yom Tov Sheni, it has the strictness of a Torah law.
Because the world has 248 limbs like a person, a Jew's Kerias Shema in New York can be the reason a Jew in Africa suddenly feels yiras Shamayim in the middle of a test.
Rosh Hashanah is the Kerias Shema of the whole year, the day's acceptance of Hashem's kingship that one prays should spread over the whole world.
A person's limbs are like the main switch of a power plant: a small movement lights up the highest worlds through a mitzvah or sets off a bomb there through a sin.
The yetzer hara lets a person eat kugel or make kiddush, but fights learning before davening; that very resistance proves its importance.
Different kinds of tzaddikim come from different limbs of Adam Harishon: the head yearns to learn like Moshe Rabbeinu, the throat to daven like Dovid Hamelech, the feet to go collecting tzedakah.
From the miracle that the Kohen Gadol never became tamei on Yom Kippur, the Mashgiach learns that the Satan fights hardest exactly where the most depends, so difficulty is a sign of one's shlichus.
Because money buys a person's food and is therefore part of his nefesh, as seen in the halachos of one forbidden to benefit from another, giving tzedakah is a kind of mesiras nefesh.

The Mashgiach draws a parallel: just as the tzaddik of the generation includes all its souls, 'v'ahavta l'reiacha kamocha' includes all the mitzvos, so accepting it binds a person to all of Klal Yisroel.
Though the first ten in shul do not hear the Shechinah speaking with them, their soul feels it, and its effect is felt through the whole day.
Saying the words of Torah she'b'chsav counts as learning even without understanding, but the beraisa of the ketores is Torah she'b'al peh, so one only fulfills learning it by knowing what it means.

The Egyptians who had seen nine plagues come true would still call Moshe a liar over a few minutes; a person who does not want to believe will deny even repeated miracles, because believing would demand changing his life.
With the Midrash on 'a thousand for each tribe', the Mashgiach explains that those who sit and learn and daven are also soldiers in the war, and saying the ketores is the Jews' 'Patriot missile'.

The Mashgiach points out that the Alter Rebbe, a strict man, chose as the harshest punishment for hasty davening being kept from hearing his Torah, which to devoted chassidim was the greatest punishment there could be.
The ridicule of long davening is itself foretold: the Gemara says that before Moshiach the G-d-fearing will be considered mad, and a tzaddik would wish his chassidim to be counted among them.

Stray thoughts in davening are not a mere lapse of attention but being pushed out of Gan Eden, like Adam HaRishon after the sin; this is why a person can find he davened half the tefillah without one word to Hashem.
The tears of real davening are tears of joy, like those of a parent and child who meet after a year apart.
Disciples of one rebbe may differ like east and west, yet all are truly his: what passes from rebbe to chassid is the point of avodah, not its outward form.
Each person lives many years but comes into the world for one day; Yosef was called Yosef HaTzaddik only after he passed his trial, and until then he was simply Yosef.
Modeh Ani precedes negel vasser even though one normally may not even attend to an optional matter before washing: the urge to thank Hashem cannot be held back.
The ten fingers are the 'control knobs' of man, who was made from all ten utterances of creation; washing them purifies the whole body and, through it, one's share in the world.
A bochur's careful negel vasser may be what keeps another Jewish bochur somewhere far away, in Paris, from sin, because each person controls a share of the world and of other souls' roots.
The Be'er Mayim Chaim reads 'arisa' (dough) as a cradle or bed: on rising from bed, the first act should be a tefillah to Hashem.
One of the great benefits of learning without a break is the training of restraint, for the yetzer works through curiosity about what is happening around.
No moment in creation is a duplicate of another; even the same mitzvah each day has a different task in fixing the world, so a missed moment cannot be made up tomorrow.
The Mashgiach reads the Sanzer Rav's words as proof that building outpaces destruction: if the Beis HaMikdash lacked only the paroches then, today it lacks only screws.

Just as a parrot's few words amaze a king more than the wisdom of his ministers, a small avodah of a weak generation is a great chiddush in heaven and is valued like the great avodos of the tzaddikim.
Because the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah composed tefillah with ruach hakodesh, the same words do a different birur every day, so a tefillah missed today cannot be made up tomorrow.
Davening fast with hishtapchus hanefesh, as the Skverer Rebbe does when davening privately, is only for one who is completely pure; ordinary people must hold on to each word.
Each word of davening is a heichal; tzaddikim can pass through quickly, but others must hold on so as not to be pushed out, and davening with a tzaddik in his minyan lets him carry them.
Raising one's voice in davening is not a show but human nature: a person shouts when he truly means something, as in an argument or at a ball game.
The severe statements of the sefarim that go beyond the Shulchan Aruch are not exaggerations: they are the halachah of a higher soul, for whom a small flaw is a real blemish.
Gan Eden and Gehinnom can be the same place: the same fiery davening of the tzaddikim is pleasure for those who trained for it and torment for those who did not.
A spiritual appetite works like a physical one: one who spoils his appetite with the pleasures of this world cannot take in the bread of Torah and tefillah.
A gift of inspiration is like the free taste of grapes the storekeeper offers: it is given to show the quality, but afterwards one must pay with toil.

Whether someone davens is a truer measure of whether he is still bound to Hashem than the severity of the punishment for a sin, just as going bareheaded marks a person though it is hard to name the sin.
Amalek's attack is coldness: 'asher karcha' means he cooled you, and the war against Amalek today is the struggle to daven with warmth.

Quoting Rabbi Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, the Mashgiach says the Ba'al Shem Tov did not hang his teaching about davening on the teivah pasuk at random: the world is a flood of desires, and tefilah is the ark that saves from it.

Amalek attaches itself to the weak souls of Dan at the edge of the camp, which hint at the lowest souls of the last generations; the defense against him is 'bo atah el hateivah', entering into tefilah.
Learning has many motives, recognition among them, while long davening only brings ridicule; this is exactly what the Gemara means when it applies 'kerum zulus' to tefilah.
Those who mock loud davening shout at Ne'ilah because they know it is a serious moment; the Mashgiach wants every tefilah to be a Ne'ilah.
The sealed ring of Bilgah is like a heart bypass: their avodah shebalev was blocked, so they had to receive from other kohanim.
Leaving right after Shemoneh Esrei is like paying for a watch and walking out without it: the shefa comes down after Shemoneh Esrei, and one must stay to take it home.
Ahavas chaverim, 'shevet achim gam yachad', is the cure for the forces of Shiva Asar b'Tammuz and the breaking of the luchos.
Following Rashi, the Mashgiach explains that in Modim d'Rabbanan we thank Hashem for the very ability to thank, and that thanking arouses heaven and opens the gates of more thanks.
Thanking Hashem for every detail is not only thanks; it is an exercise in emunah, training a person to see that nothing happens by chance.
The second rabbi at a seudas hodaah is required to show that hodaah has no end: after one chacham has finished listing reasons to thank, another still finds more.
Modim d'Rabbanan is assembled from the versions of many rabbanan, because with hodaah one person's words, even the chazzan's, can never suffice.
The korban todah's short eating time was meant to force its owner to invite more people, so that more would hear of the kindness.

The Mashgiach resolves Tosafos' question on the Rashbam by distinguishing the open leaders of a miracle from its hidden cause: Moshe and Aharon led, but the righteous women's mesirus nefesh was the hidden heart of the redemption.
Leah's thanks was new in the world because it was a mother's thanks for a child, born of her devotion to building Klal Yisroel.
Following the Kedushas Levi, even a rasha has a 'song' to Hashem: his downfall, which brings out Hashem's honor; the tzaddik, by contrast, praises Hashem while alive, through his life.
The Mashgiach reads 'with my extra being' in the passuk as 'with the gifted, extra years': these too must be used to sing to Hashem.
The Gerrer Rebbe, for whom even two lost minutes still counted half a year later, considered himself defeated by people whose need or longing outweighed his reckoning of time.
Through the korbanos of the twelve nesiim, the twelve princes of Yishmael fall, and the Mashgiach says this generation in particular must work hard in these days to push away that klipah.
Each tribe's own color on the choshen and the degel stands for a distinct middah, a distinct tafkid, and with these the nesiim of Yishmael are nullified.
Chanukas hamizbe'ach means inaugurating the avodah of the Mikdash, and since a Jew is himself a mikdash, these are days to inaugurate oneself anew.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the revealer of secrets, is the patron of the lowest souls, because he sees the secret hidden even in the lowest Jew.
Kingship, the most dangerous position for pride, is entrusted only to Yehudah, whose very name comes from thanks for receiving more than one's share.
The Korban Pesach has no chametz loaves although it is a thanks offering, because it thanks for kindness that came regardless of deeds.
Saying Modeh Ani with impure hands is itself the defeat of the kelipah: declaring that it is nothing before Hashem makes it nothing, as Avraham's dust did to the kings.
The 'king's daughter' of the kelipah is a counterfeit royalty that holds itself great, while the Jew is the true king's son whose greatness is in his smallness.
Pesach Sheini falls in the week of hod to show that even the lowest souls bring the Korban Pesach, their Modeh Ani.

The Mashgiach applies the Rambam's warning against calling troubles chance directly to the present: ignoring the Iranian threat and staying busy with trivialities is exactly the 'cruel' response the Rambam describes.
He identifies Paras of the Gemara and the Pesikta with today's Iran, the land of Achashverosh where Haman sought to kill all the Jews, and, through the Maharal, with Yishmael and Islam.

From Manoach's wife the Mashgiach derives a principle: had Hashem wanted to harm the Jews, He would not have shown them such open miracles, so the wonders in Eretz Yisrael are themselves a sign of coming salvation.
He says the miracles are not made for the Israeli government but for Klal Yisrael: those who learn Torah, keep mitzvos and will yet return.

Since sefarim say that learning Torah is Shabbos, a rest from all work, the Mashgiach argues that answering a cellphone in the middle of learning in a beis medrash brings the marketplace and the office into Shabbos and desecrates it.

Through the half shekel, where each Jew is a half and two together make one, and Korach's men whose share was not accepted because of their dispute, the Mashgiach shows that unity was the answer to Haman then and is the needed merit now.
Dveikus is explained through speech: just as two people talking together form a yichud, a union, so a Jew speaking to Hashem in tefillah is united with Him.

Tefillah's dveikus can be stronger than Torah's, because in learning one must think into the worldly matter being discussed, an ox that gored or a thief, while in davening one thinks of cleaving to Hashem.

Klal Yisroel passes through the stages of a person's life, and our generation is in its old age; like a sick man who needs orange juice rather than bread and meat, it needs the revival of tefillah more than earlier generations.
Learning to show off one's knowledge is like the young man who learned ten years for an audience that turned out to be cats.

Moshe Rabbeinu, who gave the Torah, is the head of the learners, the mind; Dovid HaMelech, who gave Tehillim, the root of all tefillos, is the head of those who daven, the heart; one who davens well binds himself to Dovid's holiness, one who learns well to Moshe's.
Whether chassidim daven quietly or loudly follows the root of the soul of their Rebbe, just as souls are sent to the Rebbe whose root they share.

Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz read the Ba'al Shem Tov's teivah as the ark against today's flood: apikorsus, desire, envy and honor drown most of the world, and the word of tefillah is where a Jew is saved.
The Mashgiach explains that saying the words of tefillah is a rabbinic mitzvah, while davening with the heart is the mitzvah of the Torah, 'to serve Him with all your heart'.
The Mashgiach notes that the Shulchan Aruch normally says what to do, yet here it narrates how early chassidim davened, because every person can reach hispashtus hagashmiyus in his own measure.
Pegiah means an appointment: if a non-Jew treats an appointment with a president as a great event, a Jew at the times of tefillah has an appointment with the King of kings.
In the story of the simple Jew, his prayer reached so deep that at 'Tzam'ah nafshi' he forgot to ask to be saved and longed only for Hashem, and he was saved.
A soul that came too late for its tikkun was measured middah k'neged middah: in its lifetime it used to come late to davening and learning.
The heading 'a song for the Shabbos day' is read as Shabbos being the singer, not the subject: no other day of the week has its own song because only Shabbos sings.

Creation in seven days is like music built from seven notes: each note alone is mere noise, the six weekdays alone are not yet music, and Shabbos completes the harp of seven strings so that the world's harmony can be sung.

The seventh of any series is its singer: the Kinneret as the seventh sea, Eretz Yisrael as the seventh land and 'chazan' of the world, the zemer as the seventh animal, and King David as the seventh of the ushpizin and 'sweet singer of Israel'.
The border of Eretz Yisrael touching the 'shoulder' of the Kinneret is read as a pat on the shoulder, the way one is praised after davening well, because the Kinneret sings the Shabbos songs.

Shabbos is tied to teshuvah because both mean returning to the root; the yovel, the 'Shabbos of Shabbosos', draws back even those too far to return on an ordinary Shabbos, like the shofar of Moshiach.

Our Shabbos is a small Shabbos that sings to the great Shabbos of the future, and a person who sees only a piece of history is like a fly on a black spot in a masterpiece, unable to see the whole picture.
A word in the chapter's last verse is written without a vav; since vav means connection, the missing letter shows that people do not see the connection and harmony in Hashem's ways.
The words 'shir l'yom' contain the letters of Yerushalayim, because the psalm is a song both to Shabbos, the Shabbos of time, and to Yerushalayim, the Shabbos of place.
The Mashgiach reads the name Chavakuk as embrace: in the last generations a Jew must hold onto emunah with all his strength.
An octave's eighth note is really the first again; a new eighth note in Moshiach's days would multiply the possible combinations, the way an eighth digit multiplies phone numbers.
The piano's seven white keys and five black keys, the sad half-tones between them, mirror the white and black experiences of life; one cannot play a beautiful melody with only one kind.
White is the color of chesed, which is why doctors traditionally wore white, carrying a spark of the angel Refael, and why the Kohanim wore white.
A drum alone is only noise, but within an orchestra it beautifies the music; so the sad times of history are part of its beauty.

The Mashgiach reads 'ki simachtani' as the joy of Shabbos rest: only when a person is free of the week's labor can he look at the harmony of creation, and that sight lets him trust that the parts he does not understand are equally deep.
'Ish ba'ar' is not an insult: even an 'ish', a person of stature, is ignorant regarding Hashem's conduct; the difference from the fool is only that the ish knows he does not know.
'Gavoha' is high but rooted in the ground, like a tall building, while 'marom' is high and detached, like a cloud; Hashem is called marom because His ways cannot be reached at all.
The wicked cannot reach the eternal Shabbos because they belong to division, like Esav's 'nafshos' in the plural, whereas Shabbos is the secret of oneness.
Oil rises above every liquid because it belongs above, and 'shemen' is linked to 'shemonah'; the Chanukah oil that was not consumed shows the eternal 'eighth' that is the existence of Klal Yisrael.

The strength of a minhag comes from the collective ruach hakodesh of Klal Yisrael, and this same hidden ruach hakodesh is what 'tishmanah oznai' describes: the Jew hears that he will outlive his enemies.

A fruit tree stays low because its roots' strength goes into the fruit, while the fruitless cedar grows tall; the tzaddik who pours himself into students is promised both the palm's fruit and the cedar's height.
The beauty of Klal Yisrael was not seen in galus because a tree only flourishes in its own soil; only when planted again 'in the house of Hashem' will the nations wonder at them.
Rosh Chodesh Teves falls on Chanukah, and a Jew lighting Chanukah lights in the street on the longest nights of a month of din is 'cutting off the head of the house of the wicked', Esav.
Tammuz's combination of the Name comes from Haman's words 'vechol zeh einenu shoveh li', with the letters fully backwards, which is why it is a month of harsher din even than Av.
'Hashem malach' in the past tense is said looking back from the days of Moshiach: then it will be clear that He reigned even in galus when His kingship was not seen.
'Gei'us lavesh' means Hashem's seeming aloofness is a garment, and the double 'lavesh ... levush' is a hiding within a hiding; but under all the garments is the Name Havayah, the Name of chessed.
The world is called 'tevel', related to 'tevel hu', a mixture; it is a world where one does not see clearly, and miracles are like lightning in a dark night.

The akeidah was hardly a test of willingness to sacrifice, since any believing Jew would obey a direct command; the test was facing Hashem's apparent contradiction of His own promise while the simple answer was hidden from Avraham.
The proof that the test was a question and not the slaughter: the posuk says Hashem tested Avraham, not Yitzchak, who was the one to be slaughtered.

The weeping of the lower waters over their distance from the King was answered by the korbanos, through which every level of creation, animal, plant and water, is brought close, and the churban renewed their weeping.
The feminine form eidosecha, rather than eidai, hints at the weakness of Israel in galus, a sheep among seventy wolves, who nevertheless remain loyal.

Edom, today's galus, includes all the earlier kingdoms, which is why Daniel saw it in a separate vision and the Torah lists the pig in a separate posuk; in America the dominant element is the galus of Yavan, the pursuit of pleasure and beauty.
The order of davening maps onto the four worlds, which is why one sits down at Yotzer: there one enters Beriah, the world of the Kisei HaKavod.
Though the generations decline, creation itself grows more elevated and souls more refined each day, so each day needs a tikkun of its own that tomorrow cannot replace.
A foreign thought during davening is not merely lost focus: it means the angels guarding that word's heichal have thrown the person out, though Hashem may admit one who toils beyond his merits.
The Mashgiach reads 'zimra' as cutting, as in pruning a vineyard: Pesukei d'Zimra cut a path through the destructive angels, because one who goes along with Dovid Hamelech cannot be stopped.
Since a person must be broken in life anyway, the drash 'shivro' teaches that it is better to be broken before Hashem, and what one suffers for Torah and avodah is subtracted from other suffering.

In the Zohar's mashal, the one who slays the serpent receives the king's daughter; the Mashgiach identifies the serpent as the yetzer hara and the king's daughter as tefillah, with its sweetness of deveikus.

Pesukei d'Zimra became obligatory because our generation is weaker, just as later generations are stricter in matters the Rishonim were lenient in, and just as the ketores once purified the air so prayers could rise.

The Mashgiach reads 'b'shem kol Yisrael' as lifting a private mitzvah into the world of Klal Yisrael, the place of Yom Kippur and of the Kodesh HaKodashim, where no accuser, angel or king can enter; strife between Jews cuts a person off from that place.

He compares l'shem yichud to the moda'ah of a coerced get: just as a prior declaration voids what follows, declaring beforehand that the mitzvah is for Hashem voids any foreign thought that later slips in, like bitul chametz.

Maaseh bereishis is 'current events': like a child who thinks the switch makes the light while the dynamos must turn every second, or a glass held in the hand that falls the moment the muscles relax, the world exists only through Hashem's constant renewal.

From 'gozer u'mekayem' the Mashgiach argues that since Hashem knows the future, a claim that He changed His mind and gave a new law cannot hold, while the giving of the Torah itself, witnessed by the whole nation, is a historical fact others cannot deny.
Because nature follows the Torah's psak, a lung that the Mechaber rules kosher can live in Eretz Yisrael, where his rulings are followed.

The Mashgiach links the new wonders of pilpul in the Acharonim, and the long teshuvos of today, with the industrial revolution and today's technology: as Jews add wonders in Torah, Hashem opens wonders in creation.
The farther a thing is from Hashem, the stronger its longing to return, like two people who love each other and are far apart; so the earth, the lowest form of creation, has the greatest longing.

The hundred daily brachos answer the angel of forgetfulness whose power reaches a hundred, the gematria of the name of the angel of forgetfulness, while 101 is the gematria of Michael, over whom forgetfulness has no hold.
The roads to Zion mourn not as a figure of speech: the very ground of the road longs to be trodden by Jews going up to Yerushalayim for a mitzvah.
Rewarding mitzvos is itself a kindness, since a person owes Hashem everything and Hashem owes him nothing; therefore 'meshalem sachar tov' is a praise of Hashem.
In Tehillim 34 and 25 the aleph-beis stands for a fixed order of reward and punishment, and the extra verse of pidyon that follows it teaches that Hashem's redemption stands above that order.

The angel created by a sin must fulfill its purpose, so when a person does teshuvah Hashem sends it to a rasha instead; this is the meaning of 'I have given Egypt as your ransom' and the secret of kaparos.

The words of Baruch Sheamar, from 'beshevachos' and 'bizmiros' through 'chai haolamim', trace the whole order of the davening that follows: Mizmor LeSodah, Pesukei Dezimra, Az Yashir, Yishtabach, Kerias Shema, Ahavah Rabbah and Shemoneh Esrei.
Mizmor LeSodah opens Pesukei Dezimra right after the brachah, just as after a brachah one first tastes the choicest fruit, and like the custom of tasting the Shabbos food on Erev Shabbos.

With a king, being called by name is a disgrace since his title is greater than his name; with Hashem it is the reverse, and His very name is the greatest praise, which is why Baruch Sheamar climbs to 'shemo hagadol'.
Thanks offered as good manners, when one feels the good was owed to him, is not hodaah; hodaah means knowing one received more than his share, which is why one bows at Modim.
Mizmor LeSodah is the hundredth psalm, corresponding to the last of the hundred daily brachos, and, as the close of Moshe Rabbeinu's eleven psalms, it is bound up with the end of days.
The Rambam's Moshiach, who shows no signs, is the greater one: a single word of his will enter every heart, so that Jews will drop everything and follow him to Eretz Yisrael.
The Mashgiach argues that headlines should be reversed: the news is not that someone starved, but that every creature has food every day.
He reads the alef-beis structure of Ashrei as a sign of the ordered balance of nature, in which each creature's eating also sustains its surroundings.
The Toldos Yaakov Yosef read 'Ashrei ha'am shekachah lo' as 'happy is the people that says: so be it', accepting everything as from Heaven.
The full spelling of 'Elokai' with a vav hints that Hashem's care fills a person's life completely, leaving no empty space.
The words of the daily prayers are like one basket carrying apples one day and potatoes the next: the same words hold different tikkunim each day.
Each Jew has one Shabbos in history that is his own, just as he has his own letter in the Sefer Torah, and how he keeps it affects all of creation.

The Mashgiach reads 'vachasidecha' as Klal Yisroel as a whole: compared to the nations, the Jewish people are the 'chasidim' of the world, and only they can bless Hashem rather than merely praise Him.
A gentile's good deed makes him a better person and earns him reward, but only a Jew's mitzvah brings shefa into the whole creation, or, the opposite, causes destruction.

'Lehodia livnei ha'adam gevurosav' is a parenthesis placed exactly halfway through the alef-beis of Ashrei: having said so many praises, David HaMelech stops to say that they only reach as far as people can grasp.

The disappearance of kingship and fear in the modern world is not an accident: the world is arranged so that there is nothing left to learn fear of Heaven from, making emunah the test of the generation.
Each of the ten makos corresponded to one of the ten maamaros, in reverse order, so that through the makos the Jews saw who created the world; from the ten makos came the ten dibros.
The 'samech' of 'somech Hashem' stands before the missing 'nun' of falling: Hashem's support comes before the fall, the cure prepared before the blow.

A tzaddik's fall is arranged from Heaven so that he goes down to a low place he would never have reached on his own and raises souls from there; this is how Hashem is 'somech' the fallen, through the tzaddik.

From 'nora alila al bnei adam' the Mashgiach shows that even the dispute between Yosef and the brothers was part of a plan leading to Egypt, the Exodus and Matan Torah, so outsiders cannot judge tzaddikim's deeds.
Tefilah is an exercise in emunah: the very act of asking awakens a person to recognize that Hashem is the provider, which is why davening for parnassa is so great.
In a time of both plague and famine, praying for food covers the plague as well, since one who is decreed sustenance must live to receive it; the Mashgiach finds this hinted in 'umasbia lechol chai'.

The decree is fixed on Rosh Hashanah, yet how much mercy accompanies it is judged each day; thus Hashem is 'tzaddik' in His decree and 'chasid' in carrying it out, and the decree can be sweetened while it remains.
A tefilah that seems unanswered is put in reserve in the heavenly account; Avraham's tefilah for Sodom was kept for later generations who would have no tzaddik great enough to daven for them.
The two halves of 'righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds' describe one decree: it is just, and yet Hashem's kindness allows a person who turns to Him in prayer to have it annulled.
The treasure of free gifts is given only to one who knows he cannot expect more than a free gift, one who is broken within himself.

Just as the word 'es' in 'he shall wash es his flesh' includes the hair that is secondary to the body, 'es kol ohavav' includes those who make themselves secondary to a tzaddik: his students and supporters.

King David ruled on questions himself before consulting Mefiboshes not from pride but because a ruling of purity from the king's mouth drew purity onto all of Klal Yisrael, which Mefiboshes' word could not.

Every creature exists to bring honor to Heaven; the tzaddik does so with his life and the rasha with his downfall, and David's 'I will praise Hashem with my life' declares that he praises in the first way.
'With my being' can mean praising Hashem even with the secondary parts of life, such as eating, sleeping and business, not only with the essential ones like prayer, Torah and tzedakah.
'A person who has no salvation' is read as one for whom the matter is not a salvation: one cannot expect someone to work for a cause that he himself does not see as a rescue.

The Mashgiach reads the order of letters in the months' names: 'aviv' runs straight forward like the chesed of Nissan, while Tishrei runs backward, as din; likewise Jews write from right to left, the side of chesed.
Whiteness is the sign of food given freely: milk for infants, who are exempt from the curse of toiling for bread, and the white manna, 'bread for nothing' from the side of chesed.
Since Noach's soul returned as Moshe, the Gemara's hint to Moshe in the word 'beshagam', said about the generation of the flood, becomes simple: Moshe was there in Noach.

Matan Torah repeated the flood, forty days against forty days, but its waters came down as Torah; the letter shin of the 'threefold Torah' added to 'mabul' makes 'b'shalom', which is why the nations were told 'Hashem will bless His people with peace'.
'Maggid' shares a root with gidim, the vessels that carry life-blood to the limbs: speech draws one's thoughts to another, and through the rain Hashem draws His word down to Yaakov.

Yitzchak could not have children until the Akeidah, where he received a new soul, and immediately afterward Rivkah's birth was announced: the Akeidah itself fulfilled the promise it seemed to contradict.
'Shamayim' comes from 'sham', 'there', the opposite of 'karov', 'here': it means the remote places, so that even the earth, seen from the heavens, is a 'there'.
The Mashgiach reads David's commanding of the heavens as more than poetry: the tzaddik, as the soul of Adam, is the key of creation, and without his song the creations cannot sing theirs.
He explains the word 'shamayim' as 'the far places', from 'sham', there: places removed from us, and 'shmei hashamayim' as what is far even from the heavens' point of view.
The harmful forces exist only on earth, since in heaven 'evil does not dwell with You', which is why the verse lists the storm wind only among the praises from the earth.
Of the four klipos in Yechezkel's vision, the 'ruach se'arah' is the worst and 'nogah' the lightest, which can be turned to holiness, like the wisdom of Yavan that can be used for kedushah.
'Hodo al eretz veshamayim' puts earth first because the praise of beings with free choice, who could refuse, is what truly shows that Hashem's name alone is exalted.
In the days of Moshiach the angels will say kadosh before the tzaddikim, so Hashem will need a new praise: this is the 'shir chadash'.
The new song of the future is like an eighth note added to the seven: as a zero added to a number multiplies it, the melodies will be enriched beyond anything possible in exile.
Singing praise for a salvation that has not yet come, out of certainty that it will, is itself the 'sword in the hand' that defeats the obstacles.

Yehuda's long retelling of what Yosef already knew was a hint to him; the descent to Egypt behind the mask of the harsh ruler is a model of the whole exile, behind which Hashem waits to reveal Himself once Israel does teshuvah.

Everything connected with 'eight' is connected with hod and hadar: on Shemini Atzeres one no longer takes the esrog because the day itself is the hadar, and the eighth day of Chanukah hints to the splendor of Moshiach.
Chesed is called gedulah because it is expansion, going out beyond the borders of oneself to another, while gevurah is contraction into oneself.
The drum has no melody and only makes noise, yet it keeps the rhythm of the whole music; so even what seems like harsh knocking in the world is a measured part of the symphony of Hashem's guidance.
Psalm 148 is praise in quantity, all creation joining; Psalm 149's 'new song' asks for quality, each creature adding something new to the praise.
Galus is not a place where Jews are stuck but a journey on the way up to Yerushalayim, so the troubles David HaMelech speaks of are stepping stones toward the Beis HaMikdash.
'Sfas sheker' is read as the edge of falsehood, like the bank of a river: one must be saved even from something on the border of a lie, in line with 'midvar sheker tirchak'.
'Lashon remiya' is what the Mashgiach calls 'politics': deceit arranged to look kosher, as one soaks and salts meat to make it kosher.
On 'mah yosif l'ba'al halashon': since speech is man's whole advantage over animals, and every animal does exactly what Hashem made it for, one who misuses speech is worse than an animal.
Tehillim 121 is the only one of the fifteen that says 'lamaalos' rather than 'hamaalos': it is a song to Hashem, who goes along with a Jew and lifts him up the steps.

Help comes 'from ayin', from nothing: when a person reaches rock bottom and can fall no lower, that itself is the sign that his salvation is coming, as the Ruzhiner's wheel parable and the Chesed L'Avraham show.

Reading 'harim' as 'horim', the Avos: Yaakov looked to his parents, who had traveled with wealth, and when he saw he had nothing, he held on to Hashem alone; the Avos' levels were taken from them so that they could set an example for their children in a fallen state.
The Mashgiach reads the second half of the verse as a consequence of the first: because the rod of the wicked cannot stay on the tzaddikim, the tzaddikim need not stretch out their hands to fight it.
The Ruzhiner held back his power against Russia as gratitude, since Russia had once let in Jews fleeing persecution, like a man who spares the robber who once gave him refuge.
The four levels of Torah, pshat, remez, drush and sod, correspond to the four levels of the soul, so a stringency in one sefer and a leniency in a posek can both be right.
A spot on a potato sack is nothing, while the same spot on silk demands a refund; so the same act that does not stain a simpler soul does stain a finer one.
The Mashgiach reads 'asher tasim lifneihem' as 'lifnim': lifnim mishuras hadin is itself a mishpat, a real law, for the one at that level.
Rav Kahana's students followed even his leniency, using hadassim that were not meshulash, to show their bond with him: hiskashrus means following the Rebbe in kulos as well as chumros.

In galus Jews do not know what they accomplish: through the Torah they gave the world, the nations slowly learned some honesty, humanity and justice, and when Moshiach comes this will be revealed and rewarded beyond what anyone dreamed.
The tefilah Moshe Rabbeinu was not allowed to say is being supplied by Jews' davening over three thousand years; when it adds up to the power of his one tefilah, the end will come.
Hashem sometimes reveals a decree precisely so that a tzaddik will daven in vain now, and the tefilah will be credited to his descendants when they need a yeshuah they do not deserve.
Haman's decree came exactly seventy years after the bowing to Nevuchadnetzar's image because those seventy years were a time of pekidah, and an eis ratzon is also when sins are recalled.
'Pedus' appears in Tanach without a vav except in 'v'harbeh imo fedus', which alludes to the full redemption of the third Beis HaMikdash.
The two alphabetical chapters of Tehillim end with an extra 'pei' verse of pedus after the alef-beis of reward and punishment, showing a conduct above strict judgment.
Just as Purim's miracle came from Hashem's chesed and not from merit, so on Purim one gives to whoever asks, and the day is called Yom Kippurim, a day 'like Purim'.
Dovid HaMelech's 'lo gavah libi' was not a lack of greatness: he simply placed all grandeur in the Beis HaMikdash rather than in his own palace.
The Mashgiach reads the destruction as only apparent: the kedushah of the Mikdash never left, and Tisha B'Av itself was meant to be a great Yom Tov.
Davening together with the chazzan is not a private act but the tefillah of the many as one, and this is the tefillah the Arizal spoke of for the last generation.
The quiet davening of Tisha B'Av may serve to show heaven what Tisha B'Av looks like when Jews do not daven aloud, so that it should no longer be a Tisha B'Av the next year.
What should be stressed as 'the main thing' depends on what has weakened: learning when learning is weak, davening when davening is weak.
Citing the Lubavitcher Rebbe, the Mashgiach notes that the fifth night, the night of hod, is the first night on which Beis Hillel's count of lights exceeds Beis Shammai's.
The two meanings of hod, admission and praise, are one: a person who feels entitled takes kindness as natural, while one who feels nothing is owed him can thank with his whole heart.
Aharon's hod, rejoicing at Moshe's appointment because he felt nothing was owed him, is why the Chanukah lights of his descendants are his lasting share.
Matisyahu, whose beis din instituted Chanukah for thanks and praise, was a spark of Yehudah, the one named for thanks and first of the degalim.
Since only thanksgiving remains in the World to Come, a person will feel there only the kind of avodah he grew used to here; Shabbos, a taste of the World to Come, is where one trains in it.
Song is a higher level than the letters themselves, since the ta'amim stand above the nekudos and the osiyos, which is why Shabbos, the day of singing, is the day of praise.
